claim: A ZFS pool's health rolls up from its top-level vdevs: all ONLINE vdevs make the pool ONLINE; any DEGRADED or UNAVAIL top-level vdev makes the pool DEGRADED; a FAULTED or OFFLINE top-level vdev makes the pool FAULTED and completely inaccessible.
stance_target: an agent can compute pool health from per-device states with a deterministic roll-up rule, no heuristics needed
scope_conditions: Oracle Solaris ZFS Administration Guide; state vocabulary shared by Linux OpenZFS
quoted_support: If all virtual devices are ONLINE, then the pool is also ONLINE. If any one of the virtual devices is DEGRADED or UNAVAIL, then the pool is also DEGRADED. If a top-level virtual device is FAULTED or OFFLINE, then the pool is also FAULTED.

claim: zpool devices fall into exactly six canonical states: ONLINE, DEGRADED, FAULTED, OFFLINE, UNAVAIL, REMOVED — with REMOVED hardware-dependent and not supported on all platforms.
stance_target: the agent's ZFS sensor should model a closed enum of device states and treat non-ONLINE as alertable
scope_conditions: zpool status output; Oracle Solaris ZFS (vocabulary inherited by OpenZFS on Linux)
quoted_support:
OFFLINE: The device has been explicitly taken offline by the administrator.

UNAVAIL: The device or virtual device cannot be opened.

REMOVED: The device was physically removed while the system was running. Device removal detection is hardware-dependent and might not be supported on all platforms.

claim: 'zpool status -x' is the machine-friendly aggregate check that prints 'all pools are healthy' when nothing needs attention, and any pool not ONLINE should be investigated.
stance_target: the cheapest reliable ZFS fleet check is zpool status -x; the agent can use it as a fast-path healthy path before parsing full status
quoted_support:
# zpool status -x
all pools are healthy

Specific pools can be examined by specifying a pool name in the command syntax. Any pool that is not in the ONLINE state should be investigated for potential problems

claim: The per-device READ, WRITE, and CKSUM columns in zpool status -v count I/O errors and uncorrectable checksum errors respectively, and non-zero values on a top-level vdev indicate potential data inaccessibility — while the 'errors:' line reports known data errors.
stance_target: agent ZFS sensors should extract per-device error counters and the errors: line as separate alert channels from pool state
quoted_support: The READ and WRITE columns provide a count of I/O errors that occurred on the device, while the CKSUM column provides a count of uncorrectable checksum errors that occurred on the device. Both error counts indicate a potential device failure, and some corrective action is needed.

claim: A DEGRADED pool continues to run with reduced redundancy or throughput, whereas a FAULTED pool is completely inaccessible until devices are attached or repaired — a two-level severity distinction an agent should preserve in its alert taxonomy.
stance_target: agent alerting should map DEGRADED to warning (system running, redundancy compromised) and FAULTED to critical (pool inaccessible)
quoted_support: A pool in the FAULTED state is completely inaccessible. No data can be recovered until the necessary devices are attached or repaired. A pool in the DEGRADED state continues to run, but you might not achieve the same level of data redundancy or data throughput than if the pool were online.

claim: ZFS pool and device failures are additionally reported by fmd (the fault manager), displayed on the system console, and logged to /var/adm/messages — on Linux OpenZFS the equivalents are zed events, meaning event-driven ZFS alerting predates and complements polling.
stance_target: agent design choice between polling zpool status vs consuming ZFS event streams (zed)
scope_conditions: Oracle Solaris fmd; Linux analogue is zed (ZFS Event Daemon)
quoted_support: In addition, potential pool and device failures are reported by fmd, displayed on the system console, and logged in the /var/adm/messages file.
